source.title: Incorporating priors in learning: a random matrix study under a teacher-student framework

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some equations and figure content have minor extraction or formatting artifacts.
record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes test risk in linear MAP regression as the dimension-to-sample ratio changes and reports a double-descent pattern near interpolation. This tests the general double-descent idea with a different model class and random-matrix analysis, not the original deep-network method.
record.gate_note: Figure 3 and the accompanying text report test risk over c=d/n for three prior and regularization settings. Figure values are not available as readable numbers, so they are recorded as figure-only. Results about risk versus regularization in Figures 1, 2, and 4 are not separate rows because they do not report the size-, epoch-, or sample-scaling behavior at issue.
record.test_reason: The paper derives and simulates test risk for linear MAP/ridge regression against c=d/n. It reports a spike at c≈1 followed by a second descent, attributes it to variance, and says regularization damps it. This is a result on V4 and part of V6 in a non-deep, linear setting, so T3 rather than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors derive exact asymptotic risks for MAP regression with Gaussian priors and say these explain double descent: a variance spike at c≈1 via 1−α→0, damped by regularization. They also give a closed-form optimal λ for c<1 with a data-driven estimator. Their emphasis is the prior–bias–variance tradeoff and optimal regularization rather than double descent itself.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a teacher–student linear MAP regression setup, random-matrix asymptotics, and simulations; it varies the dimension-to-sample ratio and prior or regularization conditions rather than scaling deep networks.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported risk landscape depends on prior quality and regularization strength; the paper also distinguishes identity covariance from general covariance.
record.peer_reviewed: IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing
record.problems: Figure 3 does not provide readable numerical values in the supplied text. The illustrated double-descent setting is linear MAP regression with identity covariance, so it does not directly establish behavior in deep networks or across other model classes.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results were left out. Figures 1, 2, and 4 report risks over regularization or estimation results rather than the scaling behavior named by the tested versions.

untested.parts: Linear regression only; no deep networks.
c=d/n is varied, but which of d or n changes is not stated. No sample-wise sweep showing more data raising risk.
Only linear MAP/ridge regression with concentrated features. Other model classes and the subsumption of the classical U-curve are untested.
No single effective-complexity measure across axes.
Noise level is not varied (σ²=0.5 fixed). No triple or multiple descent. That optimal λ removes the peak entirely is not shown; it is only said to mitigate it.

missing.what: Analytical result (Corollary 1): as λ→0, α→c, so 1−α→0 at c≈1, giving a sharp spike in train and test risk. Increasing λ raises 1−α and lowers risk. This is the paper's main evidence for double descent and its variance and regularization dependence.
missing.locator: Section 4, 'Double descent and the role of 1 − α'

missing.what: Optimal λ* is small but positive for c>1 and said to mitigate the variance explosion near c≈1. There is no curve showing peak removal under λ*.

record.verdict_notes: Double descent in ridgeless and ridge linear regression is already well established (Hastie et al., Belkin et al. are cited). This paper reproduces that result in a prior-centred generalization rather than testing it anew. All figure values are unreadable, so the evidence is the theory plus qualitative text.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses linear regression, not deep networks.
No risk sweep over training epochs or training time is reported.
Although c=d/n is varied, the study does not isolate increasing sample size near the interpolation threshold.
The reported test is in linear MAP regression; other model classes and whether the result subsumes the classical U-shaped curve are not tested.
The study does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and samples.

The text attributes the interpolation spike to variance and discusses regularization, but does not vary noise levels to test the peak mechanism, test triple or multiple descent, or show that the peak disappears under optimally tuned regularization.
The study does not recount complexity using an effective number of parameters or test whether that turns the second descent into an ordinary U shape.

rows.subject: MAP regression (identity covariance)
rows.operation_detail: Reports test risk as a function of c=d/n for the no-prior, small-regularization setting.
rows.note: The text describes a characteristic test-risk peak near the interpolation threshold followed by a decrease; no readable numerical values are provided. The paper attributes the peak to variance dominating near c≈1.
rows.check: Value is figure-only. The text states a sharp spike near c≈1 as λ→0, then a decrease for c>1. Linking is correct. It is not stated whether d or n is varied, so it cannot bear on V3.

rows.subject: MAP regression (identity covariance)
rows.operation_detail: Reports test risk as a function of c=d/n for a well-informed prior and large regularization.
rows.note: The text includes this setting among the scenarios illustrating double descent around the interpolation threshold. Numerical values are not readable.
rows.check: Large-λ setting. The theory says increasing λ grows 1−α and lowers the spike, so the peak should be attenuated. The figure is unreadable, and the text only describes the scenarios collectively. The reader's 'observed' is unsupported for this specific curve.

relationships.condition: Linear MAP regression, Σ=I, no prior, small λ
relationships.reason: R1 and the closed-form analysis show a test-risk spike at c≈1 (1−α→0), then a decrease for c>1. This is a non-deep model class.
relationships.display_finding: Test risk spiked near c = 1 as 1 − α approached zero, then decreased for c > 1.

relationships.condition: Linear MAP regression, Σ=I; variance mechanism and regularization damping (analytical)
relationships.reason: The text attributes the spike to variance via the 1/(1−α) term and says larger or optimal λ damps it. This verdict rests mainly on the text and theory; R1 shows the small-λ spike.
relationships.display_finding: The variance term 1/(1−α) generated the spike, which larger or optimal λ damped.
